Long, long ago, in the little town of Bethlehem, there lived a big family, and the youngest of eight brothers was named David. He watched over the sheep on the green hills and played for them on his little harp. The sheep would listen — and even the lambs stopped hopping about.

One day, old Prophet Samuel came to Bethlehem to choose the future king. Seven tall brothers passed before him, but the prophet only shook his head. "There's still the youngest," they told him, "he's out with the sheep." And it was David whom Samuel chose — for what matters isn't how you look on the outside, but what kind of heart you have.

Watching sheep was no quiet job. Sometimes a lion crept close, sometimes a bear. But David never ran away — he protected every single sheep, even the smallest one. That's how the little shepherd learned to be brave, long before his great and mighty deeds.

Meanwhile, enemies called the Philistines had attacked the land. Every morning a giant named Goliath came out of their camp — tall as a tree, his armor gleaming like a shiny copper pot. “Who will fight me?” he roared. For forty days, no one dared to answer.

One day David's father sent him to take bread and cheese to his brothers at the camp. That was when the boy heard Goliath's thundering voice. All the soldiers looked down at the ground. But David asked, "Why doesn't anyone stop this giant?"

"I will go," said David. King Saul gave him his own armor: the helmet slid right down over the boy's nose, and the chainmail hung all the way to his feet. "This won't do at all," laughed David. "I'll go just as I am. I have what's always with me: my sling and a faithful heart."

At the stream, David chose five smooth stones — just the kind that fit snugly in a sling. He put them in his shepherd's bag, stretched the sling's strap, and set off into the valley. A little shepherd boy — off to face a giant.

Goliath laughed out loud at the sight of the boy. But David calmly loaded his sling, whirled it round — whoosh! — and the stone flew straight to its mark, and the giant crashed down like a chopped tree. It only took one stone — and a whole lot of courage.

After his victory, David was invited to live in the palace. Whenever King Saul felt sad, David played the harp for him — and the sadness melted away, like morning mist. And the king's son, Jonathan, became David's truest friend in all the world.

But David's fame gave the king no peace. Saul grew so jealous that David had to leave the palace and hide away in the mountains. Was that unfair? Oh, very much so. But David held no grudge, and simply waited for the king's heart to soften.

One day Saul, chasing after David, stopped to rest in the very cave where David was hiding. There he was — the one who wanted to harm him, so close! But David only quietly snipped off a little piece of the king's robe: "I could have — but I didn't." Kindness is stronger than revenge.

Years passed, and David became king. He made the hilltop city of Jerusalem his capital. The city was decorated and surrounded with walls, and it shone like the crown of the land. Even today, it is called the City of David.

But the crown couldn't silence the music. In the evenings, King David would pick up his harp and write songs — psalms: about stars, about courage, about gratitude. These songs are three thousand years old, and people still sing them today — now that's a hit song!

David dreamed of building a great Temple in Jerusalem — the most beautiful house on earth. But he heard, “It is not you who will build it, but your son.” David wasn't upset: he gathered stones, gold, and plans, so his son would have something to start with. Knowing how to prepare the way for someone else is a great thing too.

Even great kings make mistakes — and David made them too. But he knew how to do something harder than winning any battle: to say “I was wrong” — and set things right. There's no shame in admitting you were wrong. The real shame is pretending you weren't.

When David grew old, he passed the kingdom on to his son, Solomon. "Be strong and be kind," he told him. "And may you have wisdom enough for two." Looking ahead a little: Solomon ended up with wisdom enough for the whole world.

And that's how a little shepherd boy with a harp became a great king. Not because he was taller or stronger than everyone else — but because he had a brave and kind heart. And David's songs are still sung today. Maybe one day you'll sing them too.
